wine.name: Prestige Brut
wine.grapes: Furmint and Chardonnay; earlier releases were mostly Furmint, and the estate's own recent sheet gives Chardonnay the larger part.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards on the slopes of Somló, a lone extinct volcano whose old lava flows left basalt over the hill.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, the second fermentation taking place in the bottle, in the sparkling wine cellar the estate completed in 2011, with a cellar master from Champagne advising from the start. The wine rests on its lees for at least two years before disgorging, three years and more by the estate's recent sheet, and is finished Brut.
wine.glass: Lemon peel and pear with brioche from the long time on the lees, a fine, persistent mousse and a taut, salty finish of grapefruit pith carried by the high acidity of the hill.
wine.ageing: Ready on release and made to be drunk within a few years of disgorging, though a bottle kept a while longer gains toast and depth.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; never decanted; a tulip or white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: Hungarian for sparkling wine, the word on the back label.
Dry: only a little sugar is added in the dosage after disgorging.
The protected name of the wider district: Somló hill with the smaller hills of Ság and Kis-Somló.

records.table: Kreinbacher is the Somló estate that set out in 2002 to make bottle fermented sparkling wine on a volcanic hill known for its still white wines. Its Prestige Brut blends Furmint with Chardonnay and rests years on its lees; pour it cold as an aperitif.
records.story: Somló was known for still white wine, lean and smoky Juhfark and Furmint from the basalt of a lone extinct volcano. In 2002 a founder whose family name the house carries bought his first vineyards on the hill with a plan to make sparkling wine fermented in the bottle there. The plan needed a cellar built for it, and in 2011 the estate completed its headquarters, winery and sparkling wine cellar, buildings set into an artificial hill shaped to blend with the slopes of the volcano. A cellar master from Champagne has advised on the sparkling wines from the start, and the sparkling wines made there were released from 2014. Furmint, long grown on the hill, gave the wines their Hungarian accent, with Chardonnay beside it, while the estate kept making still Juhfark from the same slopes. Magyar Bor, the national wine body, holds the house up to show that basalt and Furmint can make sparkling wine without the limestone of Champagne. For a sommelier, Prestige Brut is the bottle that shows Somló's acidity in a new form: proof that a hill famous for slow, smoky still whites can also make a long aged sparkling wine.

The share of Furmint has moved between releases, so a bottle's back label, not habit, says which grape leads.

wine.name: Aranyhegy Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape, named for its long, tight bunch shaped like a sheep's tail.
wine.sites: Aranyhegy, the golden hill, one of the house's named vineyards on the southern side of Somló, on the volcanic soils of the hill.
wine.making: Picked from Aranyhegy alone, then fermented and aged in oak barrels as one of the house's Selection wines, its single vineyard tier raised in wood. The time in barrel moves with the vintage, so none is given here.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon peel and quince over a smoky, flinty note from the volcanic soil, with restrained fruit, firm, tangy acidity and a long saline finish; honey and nuttiness come with years in bottle.
wine.ageing: Taut and closed when young; like all Juhfark it needs several years in bottle to round its acidity and show its honeyed depth, and it keeps well beyond that.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Tornai is the Somló family house that traces its start to 1946, and its Aranyhegy Juhfark is the hill's own grape from one named vineyard, fermented in oak. It is smoky, saline and high in acid, so give it years and a cool glass.
records.story: Somló is a lone extinct volcano in the flat country north of Lake Balaton, and its wines were long prized in the Habsburg lands; a claim often repeated says Empress Maria Theresa (1717 to 1780) favoured them, and folk legend made Juhfark the wine of the wedding night, said to bring a son and heir. Tornai traces its start to 1946, when its founder began with a small plot on the hill. Private winemaking in Hungary grew again after the change of regime in 1990, and in the decades that followed the family gathered vineyards across the southern slopes, Aranyhegy and Grófi among them, and Magyar Bor, the national wine body, counts Tornai among the larger houses making Juhfark. In 2021 the estate marked seventy five years on the hill. The house makes Juhfark at several levels, from a fresh Somlói bottling to wines of a single named vineyard. For a sommelier, the Aranyhegy Juhfark is the sheep's tail grape shown by one site, the way Somló's growers have long named their slopes.

wine.name: Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape of the long, sheep's tail bunch.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the south-eastern side of Somló, around the Apátság vineyard, on the volcanic soils of the hill.
wine.making: Pressed after six to twelve hours on the skins and fermented with wild yeast in wood, then aged in large old casks of oak and acacia for at least a year, two to three years by one importer's account. Some bottlings carry the name of the cask that raised them.
wine.glass: Quince, baked apple and lemon peel over smoke, wet stone and salt, with a broad, textured middle from the skin contact, high acidity and a long, slightly bitter almond finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and reserved for its first years, it is made to age: a good bottle develops over ten years and more, turning honeyed and nutty.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Sheep's tail: the grape is named for the long shape of its bunch.

records.table: Kolonics is a small family cellar on the slope of Somló that works in the old way, with skin contact, wild yeast and long ageing in large oak and acacia casks. Its Juhfark is smoky, salty and slow to open, so pour it cool and give it air.
records.story: Kolonics is a family winery on the south-eastern slope of Somló whose history, by its own account, reaches back several generations. The first cellar came into the family in the late nineteenth century, when a great grandfather, a postmaster by trade, bought it, and much later the parents of the present winemaker gave it to him as a graduation gift. The family's own first wines followed in 2000, and the main building at the centre of the estate opened in 2008. The winemaker is the fourth generation at the head of the family's estate and learnt its methods from his father and grandfather: grapes left a few hours on their skins, fermentation with wild yeast, and long rest in large old casks of oak and acacia before bottling. Some Juhfark bottlings take the names of their casks, named for chieftains of early Hungarian history such as Álmos. In 2017 its Somlói Juhfark of the 2015 vintage was chosen as a category winner of the Wine of the Hungarian Parliament. The family grows the hill's whites alone: Juhfark, Furmint, Hárslevelű and Olaszrizling among them. For a sommelier, Kolonics's Juhfark is the old Somló style, broad, smoky and saline, made to wait.

traps: A Kolonics Juhfark named for a cask, such as Álmos, is Juhfark all the same: the name is the cask's, not a grape or a place.
Acacia here is the wood of the casks, a Hungarian tradition, not a flower note promised in the glass.

wine.name: Somlói Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape, named for its bunch shaped like a sheep's tail.
wine.sites: The house's small holding on the southern side of Somló, in the Aranyhegy and Szent Márton vineyards, on the basalt and volcanic soils of the hill.
wine.making: Fermented with its own wild yeast in used Hungarian oak casks of about a thousand litres and aged in them for about a year, then rested further in stainless steel. In the cellar's long habit the wines stay three to four years at the house before they are released.
wine.glass: Quince, ripe pear and lemon peel over smoke, flint and salt, with a firm, tangy acidity, a broad texture from the long rest and a long, savoury finish that turns honeyed and nutty with age.
wine.ageing: Released already a few years old, it is firm even then and opens further over many years in bottle, as the hill's Juhfark is known to do.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour to let it open; a white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Fekete is the small Somló cellar of an old winegrower known on the hill as its grand old man, and its Somlói Juhfark keeps his slow way: wild yeast, large used casks and years at the house before release. Pour it cool and give it time.
records.story: Fekete began in the early 1980s by the cellar's own account, in the early 1970s by others, when its founder, a winegrower who would become known on Somló as the hill's grand old man, set out on a small holding on the southern side of the hill and slowly enlarged it. He made white wine alone, from the hill's old grapes, Juhfark and Hárslevelű above all, with Furmint and Olaszrizling beside them, and he kept to the slow ways of the old cellars: fermentation with the wine's own yeast, large used casks and years of rest at the house before a wine was sold. In time his wines were among the Somló bottles that foreign writers and buyers sought out, a Juhfark of the 2008 vintage among those a British writer noted, and his Juhfark and Hárslevelű became the wines the house was known by. In 2014 the founder retired and passed the cellar to new owners, a small group of partners who bought it from him and set out to keep his methods and his style. The house has kept to releasing its wines only after three or four years in the cellar. For a sommelier, Fekete's Somlói Juhfark is the hill's grape as one of its older growers made it: patient, smoky and saline.

wine.name: Nagy-Somlói Juhfark
wine.grapes: Juhfark alone, the hill's own white grape, named for its bunch shaped like a sheep's tail.
wine.sites: The old abbey vineyard around the cellar on the south-eastern slope of Somló, put back together from more than twenty small parcels after 2001.
wine.making: Fermented with wild yeast in Hungarian oak casks and aged in the same wood, with nothing added in the cellar but the sulphur the wine needs, by the cellar's own account; the vineyard is farmed organically, from 2017 by that account.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, green pear and quince over smoke, wet stone and sea salt, lean and taut, with a firm line of acidity and a long, slightly bitter finish of almond skin.
wine.ageing: Tight and austere when young, it needs a few years to round its acidity and keeps well for a decade, gaining honey and nuttiness.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Of the abbey: the cellar and its vineyard once belonged to a Benedictine abbey.
Cellar: the Hungarian word for a winery's cellar and its house.

records.table: Somlói Apátsági Pince is the old abbey cellar of Somló, revived in 2001 on the vineyard the Benedictines of Pannonhalma once held. Its Nagy-Somlói Juhfark is wild fermented in Hungarian oak, lean, smoky and saline; pour it cool and give it time.
records.story: For centuries the church held vineyards on Somló, and several abbeys kept cellars on the hill, the Cistercians of Zirc among them. By the cellar's own account, the Benedictine Archabbey of Pannonhalma held vines on the hill from 1811 and in 1901 bought the land that gives the cellar its name, working it through its own vintner, a man of the Fazekas family. In 1948, when the communist state nationalised the lands of the religious orders, the abbey's vineyard was broken up into small parcels, and the cellar with the little plot below it went to the vintner's family. In 2001 a group of partners bought the cellar building from that family and set about putting the old abbey vineyard back together from more than twenty parcels, replanting it with the hill's own white grapes. They named the house for the abbey, kept the old cellar, and work with wild yeast and Hungarian oak, and in 2017 they turned the vineyard to organic farming. For a sommelier, the abbey cellar's Juhfark is a reminder that the church shaped Somló's vineyards for centuries, and that a vineyard scattered under communism could be made whole again.

traps: Somlói Apátsági Pince is not run by monks: the abbey held the vineyard until 1948, and a private house revived it in 2001.
The abbey of the cellar's name is Pannonhalma, the Benedictine archabbey, not Tihany or Zirc, though the Cistercians of Zirc also kept a cellar on the hill.

questions.q: A guest asks how Somlói Apátsági Pince makes its Nagy-Somlói Juhfark. Which answer fits?
opts: Wild yeast fermentation in Hungarian oak casks
Cultured yeast in temperature controlled steel tanks
Fermentation in clay amphorae buried in the ground
Grapes dried on mats before a slow fermentation
questions.exp: The cellar ferments with wild yeast in Hungarian oak and adds nothing but sulphur; it does not work in steel with cultured yeast.

questions.q: In what year did new owners buy the old abbey cellar on Somló and start to rebuild its vineyard?
questions.exp: They bought the cellar from the vintner's family in 2001; 1948 is the year the abbey's vineyard was nationalised and broken up.

report: The tie to Pannonhalma is confirmed by the cellar's own history and a presentation of its own; the year of the archabbey's purchase is not clear from the search summaries (1901 or 1911, with a sale of 1911 for 53,800 korona), so the story says early in the twentieth century and names 1911 only as a recorded sale; a refuter should read the cellar's history page itself.
The founding partner of 2001 is living and is not named; neither is the vintner's grandson, who by the cellar's account still works in it.
The plan's doubt is answered: the house's Juhfark is the wine every trade page read shows first, and its own history ties it to Pannonhalma, so no swap is proposed.
Founded is 2001, the year the present house bought the cellar and began, as Magyar Bor's and the cellar's own pages give it; the cellar itself is older and its building date was not found.
The making is the cellar's own general account (Hungarian oak, wild yeast, sulphur alone, organic since 2017); no sheet for the Juhfark alone was found, so no time in cask is given.
The south-eastern aspect rests on the importer's note and Kolonics's address in the same Apátság vineyard.
